title: Continuous batching
tagline: Keep every GPU slot busy by swapping requests in and out at every token step.
explain:
Generating text is sequential: each new token needs one forward pass. A GPU is most efficient when many sequences share a pass, because the cost of reading model weights from memory is paid once for the whole batch.

Static batching groups N requests and runs until all finish. Short requests finish early and their slots idle while the longest one completes, so utilization collapses when output lengths vary.

Continuous (in-flight) batching schedules at the granularity of a single decode step: the moment a sequence finishes, its slot is given to a waiting request. New prompts are prefilled and join the running batch. Throughput rises several times with no change in output quality.

Related techniques:

- PagedAttention stores the KV cache in small blocks like virtual memory pages, removing fragmentation and allowing prefix sharing.
- Chunked prefill splits long prompts so they do not stall token generation for other users.
- Prefill/decode disaggregation runs the compute-bound prompt phase and memory-bound decode phase on different GPU pools.
- Admission control and queues keep latency bounded when demand exceeds capacity.

Metrics: time to first token (TTFT), inter-token latency, tokens per second per GPU, and queue time. Throughput and latency trade off through batch size.
tradeoffs: Bigger batches raise throughput and cost efficiency but lengthen per-request latency.
Chunked prefill smooths latency for others but slows the long prompt itself.
pitfalls: Benchmarking with equal-length requests (hides the benefit).
Ignoring KV cache memory when raising max batch size.
interview: Why does continuous batching beat static batching?
What limits your concurrent requests on a GPU?

title: KV cache and serving capacity
tagline: Why LLM serving is a memory problem.
explain:
During generation, attention needs the keys and values of every previous token. Recomputing them each step would be quadratic, so they are cached per layer. This KV cache grows linearly with context length and with the number of concurrent requests.

Per-token size = 2 (K and V) x layers x kv_heads x head_dim x bytes. Total per request multiplies by context length. For a 70B model with grouped-query attention (8 KV heads) in fp16 that is about 330 KB per token, so an 8k-token request holds ~2.6 GB. After weights are loaded, KV cache space decides how many requests fit concurrently.

Levers:

- Grouped-query / multi-query attention shrink kv_heads (8x savings is common).
- Quantize the KV cache to FP8 or INT8 (halves memory, small quality risk).
- PagedAttention eliminates waste from over-allocation.
- Prefix caching shares KV blocks across requests with an identical prefix (system prompts, few-shot examples), cutting both memory and prefill time.
- Sliding-window or sparse attention bound the cache; offloading to CPU or NVMe for idle sessions.
- Context compaction at the application level (summaries) reduces tokens sent at all.

Capacity planning uses this math: max concurrent requests = (GPU memory - weights - overhead) / KV per request.
tradeoffs: Long contexts are expensive in memory, which is why price per token often rises with context.
Quantizing the cache saves memory at some risk to long-range accuracy.
pitfalls: Assuming multi-head cache sizes when the model uses GQA, or vice versa.
interview: Compute KV cache per token for a given model config.
How would you double concurrency without adding GPUs?

title: The RAG pipeline and hybrid retrieval
tagline: Each stage fixes a specific failure of the stage before it.
explain:
Retrieval-augmented generation lets a model answer from your data. The online path:

1. Query understanding: rewrite follow-ups into standalone queries, expand abbreviations, optionally split multi-part questions.
2. Retrieve: run dense (embedding) and sparse (BM25) search in parallel with tenant and permission filters. Dense finds paraphrases; BM25 finds exact names, codes and rare terms.
3. Fuse: reciprocal rank fusion combines rankings without calibrating scores: score = sum of 1 / (60 + rank).
4. Rerank: a cross-encoder reads query and passage together and re-scores the top 50. Slower, far more accurate.
5. Pack context: select the best 6-10 passages, order them (best first and last), add titles and source ids, respect the token budget.
6. Generate with instructions to cite and to abstain when evidence is missing.

The offline path: parse documents, chunk with structure, enrich chunks with context and metadata, embed, and index (vector plus keyword), with incremental updates and delete propagation.

Debugging order: is the answer in the corpus, in the top 50, in the top 8, and did the model use it? Measure recall@k for retrieval and faithfulness for generation separately, on a golden set from real queries.
tradeoffs: Rerankers and query rewriting add latency (often 100-400 ms) for notable quality gains.
Larger chunks keep context but dilute embeddings; smaller chunks are precise but lose surrounding meaning.
pitfalls: Tuning prompts when retrieval is the real problem.
interview: Your RAG answers are wrong. Walk through the diagnosis.
Why use hybrid search and a reranker?

title: The agent loop and its guardrails
tagline: A model in a loop with tools, wrapped by deterministic safety code.
explain:
An agent repeats: the model reads the conversation and tool results, decides on a tool call or a final answer, the runtime executes the tool, and the result is appended to the context. It stops when the model answers or a limit fires.

What makes it reliable is everything around the model:

- Budgets: maximum steps, tokens, wall-clock time and spend per run.
- Loop detection: hash repeated tool calls and intervene or abort.
- Tool design: narrow, well-described tools; helpful error messages the model can act on; truncated, relevant outputs.
- Policy layer: deterministic permission checks, argument validation, allow-lists and human approval for risky actions, enforced outside the model.
- Idempotency keys so retried side effects happen once.
- State and checkpoints so a crash resumes mid-run.
- Context management: compaction, notes, sub-agents.
- Verification: tests, schema checks or a second model before committing results.
- Tracing for every step so failures can be diagnosed and turned into evals.

Reliability compounds: 0.95 success per step over 20 steps is only 36%. Prefer fewer steps, workflows over agents where the path is known, and checks after risky steps.
tradeoffs: Autonomy raises capability and variance; add human checkpoints for irreversible actions.
More tools give more power but make selection harder; consolidate overlapping tools.
pitfalls: Relying on the prompt for safety.
No budget, so one stuck run costs hundreds of dollars.
Returning huge tool outputs that flood the context.
interview: Design an agent that can issue refunds safely.
How do you debug an agent that picks the wrong tool?
